 SUPREME COURT OF SINGAPORE 26 November 2025 Case Summary da Silveira, Virgilio Tarrago and another v Hashstacs Pte Ltd and another [ 2025] SGCA(I) 3 Court of Appeal Civil Appeal from the Singapore International Commercial Court No 1 of 2025 -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Decision of Steven Chong JCA, Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA and Arjan Kumar Sikri IJ (grounds of decision delivered by Belinda Ang Saw Ean JCA): Outcome: the Court of Appeal (the “Court” ) dismissed an appeal against the decision of the International Judge (the “Judge” ) sitting in the Singapore International Commercial Court and in doing so affirmed the Judge’s dismissal of the appellants’ claims in fraudulent and/or negligent misrepresentation against the first respondent. The Court also ordered default indemnity costs against the appellants in respect of their appeal. Factual Background 1 The appellants were the claimants in a misrepresentation claim before the Judge below, instituted against the first respondent alone. The first appellant ( “Mr da Silveira” ) was a British citizen residing in Cyprus and the sole director and shareholder of the second appellant which he incorporated as a special purpose vehicle in Cyprus ( “Munchetty” ). 2 The first respondent was a Singapore-incorporated company named Hashstacs Pte Ltd. It was the wholly-owned subsidiary of a British Virgin Islander (BVI) entity named Hashstacs Inc. The former is referred to in the Court’s grounds of decision as “Hashstacs (SG)” and the latter as “Hashstacs (BVI)” to distinguish them. The second respondent ( “Mr Soh” ) was the director of Hashstacs (SG), a material witness in the trial below, and a defendant in the appellants’ actions in unjust enrichment and conspiracy, which were dismissed by the Judge below and not appealed against. Another material witness for the respondents in the trial below ( “Mr  Cowan” ) was the founder and the Group Chief Executive Officer of a Gibraltarian entity ( “GSX” ) . GSX was the majority shareholder in Hashstacs (BVI). 3 The misrepresentation claims stemmed from a number of statements drawn from two sources – first, the third whitepaper published in relation to a blockchain technology project known as the “STACS Protocol” on or around 18 March 2019 (the “Third Whitepaper” ) (the “Whitepaper Representations” ); second, a website which was a product launching page of the STACS Protocol (the “STACS Website” ) (the “Website Representations ) . The representations related inter alia to statements that, when the hybridised STACS Protocol project was implemented and began to earn transaction fees on a private permissioned blockchain mechanism for verified partners ( “Native STACS” ) and an open publicly accessible blockchain system for the clearing of trades in digital securities and assets worldwide (the “Global STACS” ) , the receipts would be distributed in a given manner, including by using 80% of those receipts to purchase the STACS Protocol’s utility token ( “STACS Token s” ) from the open market , which had a limited quantity of 900 million STACS Tokens. 4 Mr da Silveira’s evidence below was that he saw the representations sometime in or around March–April 2019. Induced by those representations, he decided to purchase STACS Tokens from 15 August 2019 to 5 December 2019 (the “Transacted STACS Tokens” ). In September 2020, he transferred his legal title to the Transacted STACS Tokens to Munchetty, but he asserted that he retained the beneficial interest in them. 5 In the first quarter of 2019, the Native STACS was implemented in a limited fashion. The Global STACS was never implemented. According to Mr Cowan’s unchallenged evidence below, that was on account of regulatory issues arising from GSX’s unsuccessful talks with the Gibraltarian financial services regulator. Thereafter, Mr Cowan decided to change GSX’s business model by inter alia replacing the STACS Protocol project with a new project known as “GATENet” which was said to overcome a number of regulatory and other obstacles in the STACS Protocol model. As part of that shift, a one-to-one swap was effected between the old STACS Tokens and the new “Gate Tokens” , with new Gate Tokens being air-dropped to the private wallets of existing STACS Tokens holders around January 2021 ( “Token Swap” ), and with the old STACS Tokens ceasing to have any further utility thereafter. 6 The appellants’ case below was based on various causes of action. On the torts of deceit and negligent misrepresentation, the appellants pleaded that Hashstacs (SG) made fraudulent or negligent misrepresentations that led to Mr da Silveira’s purchase of the STACS Tokens. The Token Swap allegedly showed that the appellants’ pleaded representations were false and fraudulently or negligently made. The appellants had suffered consequential economic loss as a result of the Token Swap. The first respondent’s defence below was that inter alia it did not make the pleaded representations, which had been made by Hashstacs (BVI) and/or GSX instead. 7 Following the trial below, the Judge dismissed the appellants’ claims in toto in misrepresentation against the first respondent and unjust enrichment and conspiracy against both respondents. Among other findings, the Judge held that – (1) Hashstacs (SG) could not be regarded as the maker of the Whitepaper Representations, because he accepted the evidence of Mr Soh and Mr Cowan that employees of Hashstacs (SG) had edited the Third Whitepaper and made them available on the STACS Website on the instructions of Mr Cowan and solely for the benefit of Hashstacs (BVI) and GSX, and there was no need to go on to separately consider the Website Representations; and (2) in the alternative, if Hashstacs (SG) had been the maker of the Whitepaper Representations, he would have found one aspect of them to be actionable in tort, viz , the undertaking as to how transaction fees received from the STACS Protocol would come to be distributed, subject to the caveat that it was viable to implement the STACS Protocol and the project proved to be commercially successful. He awarded costs to the respondents jointly payable by the appellants in instalments. 8 The appellants did not appeal against the Judge’s dismissal of their claims in unjust enrichment and conspiracy, but they did appeal against the dismissal of their claims in fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation. The Court’s grounds of decision The appellants failed to prove that the first respondent was either the representor of the pleaded representations or had adopted and ratified their contents as its own 9 The Court agreed with the Judge’s exposition on the law on the tort of deceit, the first ingredient being that there must be a representation of fact made by words or conduct by the defendant, or alternatively, the defendant manifestly approved and adopted the representation of a third party (at [7 3]–[74] ). The applicable legal test was whether, on an objective assessment of the totality of Hashstacs (SG)’s words or conduct, in all the circumstances, a reasonable person would have considered that Hashstacs (SG) was a maker of the pleaded representations or, alternatively, it approved and adopted those representations which had been made by another person (at [78]–[80] ). 10 Applying that legal test to the facts concerned, the Judge was correct in accepting the consistent evidence of Mr Soh and Mr Cowan that everything done by employees of Hashstacs (SG) in relation to the Third Whitepaper, viz , editing the Third Whitepaper and making it available to the public on the STACS Website in March 2019, was done on the instructions of Mr Cowan and performed for the benefit of Hashstacs (BVI) and GSX. The appellants had not put to either witness in the trial below that this evidence was false and hence they were precluded by the rule in Browne v Dunn from submitting that their evidence should not be believed (at [ 81]–[89] ). 11 On the question whether the acts of the employees of Hashstacs (SG) as described above would objectively constitute it a maker of the Whitepaper Representations (at [90] ) , the Court agreed with the Judge that Hashstacs (SG) was not the maker. Having regard to the facts and considerations of authorial and editorial control and control over the process of publication, a reasonable person in the position of the representee would come to the view inter alia that all acts of Hashstacs (SG)’s employees in editing and uploading the Third Whitepaper were not performed for its own ends but only for Hashstacs (BVI), and that Hashstacs (BVI) had control of the STACS Website in the substantive sense of controlling the contents uploaded thereupon. The Judge correctly accorded weight to the facts that the Third Whitepaper made no mention of Hashstacs (SG), named Hashstacs (BVI) on the cover page as its publisher, was written from the perspective of GSX as the persona, and expressly identified GSX and Hashstacs (BVI) as the service-providers in relation to the STACS Protocol which were capable of fulfilling the Whitepaper Representations, a fact confirmed by the commercial background surrounding the STACS Protocol that evidenced that it was GSX which owned and controlled the STACS Protocol and not Hashstacs (SG). The Court, in rejecting the appellants’ argument, concluded from Hashstacs (SG)’s words or conduct that it never made the Whitepaper Representations and had not adopted its contents as its own (at [91]–[98] ). 12 On the Website Representations, the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proof that Hashstacs (SG) was the maker of the Website Representations. The only evidential basis adduced therefor was a screenshot in Mr da Silveira’s witness statement. On his oral evidence, he had never seen the original source of that screenshot and he could not provide the full context in which the Website Representations had originally been found. That context was critical in determining the identity of the maker of the Website Representations, having regard to the words or conduct of Hashstacs (SG) in the totality of their circumstances. That evidential gap was resolved against the appellants (at [ 100]–[104] ). 13 As the appellants failed to show that Hashstacs (SG), by its words or conduct, made or adopted the pleaded representations, the Court dismissed the appellants’ appeal on that ground (at [104]– [105] ). The pleaded representations were either not proven to have been made or did not amount to actionable representations of past or present fact 14 Additionally, the Court found the appellants were not entitled to succeed in their claim in misrepresentation for a second reason, viz , the first ingredient of the tort of deceit at [ 9] above was not met because the pleaded representations were not representations of fact. In particular, a representation of fact requires that the representation be one of past or present fact, capable of being true or false at the time it was made. In contrast, where the representation concerns only future facts or the representor’s future conduct, it is not capable of being true or false at the time, reflecting either a belief or opinion as to the future, an aspiration to make it come true, or a promise to perform as stated in the future. While a promise as to the future may give rise to liability in contract law, it is not actionable in the tort of deceit (at [10 6] and [108] –[110] ). 15 To determine whether the pleaded representations were representations of fact, the Court first assessed which representations were objectively shown to have been made in the first place, applying the reasonable person test as at [9] above (at [ 111] ). Based on that legal test, the Court found that two of the Whitepaper Representations had not been made, as their pleaded contents did not cohere with the contents of the Third Whitepaper looked at in the full context of that document (at [112]–[ 118] ). In contrast, three of the Whitepaper Representations cohered with an objective reading of the Third Whitepaper’s contents, viz , that the STACS Tokens would be the utility token powering the ecosystem of the STACS Protocol, that verified partners would be required to “stake” a minimum number of STACS Tokens to enjoy such rights as access to the Native STACS, and transaction fees earned on the STACS Protocol would be distributed in a promised fashion, with 80% being used to purchase STACS Tokens from the open market (the “Representations” ) (at [ 119]–[120] ). 16 None of the three Representations were representations of fact. They did not concern any past or present facts but were representations of the future conduct of the maker in relation to the prospective operation of the STACS Protocol. That was shown upon reading the Representations in the full context of the Third Whitepaper, with the totality of its contents evidencing that it was describing a future project that had yet to be fully implemented, representing an aspirational vision of the maker(s) that they envisaged to be brought to fruition in the ideal state of affairs. The Representations were therefore not representations of fact and were not actionable in tort as misrepresentations (at [122]–[ 126] ). The Court was, with respect, not able to concur with the Judge’s views, expressed in the alternative at [ 7] above, that the Representations were capable of being false if the undertaking as to the distribution of the transaction receipts was not implemented as promised in the event the STACS Protocol proved viable to implement and a success. Such a caveated undertaking was not reconcilable with the proper analysis that the Representations were actionable only to the limited extent it impliedly represented a then-present fact as to the state of mind of the maker(s) and their genuine intent to implement the STACS Protocol project as described, being restricted to their state of mind solely at the time of their making. The Representations remained true even if there was a genuine change of heart thereafter (at [ 127]–[136] ). 17 As for the Website Representations, the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proof based on Mr da Silveira’s screenshot at [12] above. That screenshot did not show the context in which the Website Representations were made to shed light on how they would reasonably have been understood. The appellants failed to prove their objective meaning. In any event, the Website Representations clearly pertained only to the future (at [121] ). Conclusion 18 The appellants’ civil appeal was dismissed with default indemnity costs being ordered against them. The usual consequential orders applied (at [ 137]–[138] and [140] ).
